The phone is social engineering’s new goldmine
items.summary: The gold standard of cybersecurity awareness used to be teaching people not to click on suspicious links. We learned to look for typos in sender addresses, spot clunky logos, and hover over URLs before taking the bait. But as automated filters and human scepticism started securing traditional email phishing, threat actors pivoted. They didn’t invent a new tactic; they simply picked up the phone. Voice phishing, or vishing, has quietly transformed from an annoyance into one of the most prolific social engineering issues facing people and companies today. The reason is simple: while we have been trained to treat our email inboxes with suspicion, we are still quite casual when it comes to our phones. The quick rise in vishing is fuelled by a perfect storm of psychology, systemic vulnerability and deepfakes. The psychological hack Where emails generally give the recipient time to pause, reflect and verify, a phone call does the opposite. It usually demands immediate attention and triggers an instinctual urge to respond. When a voice on the line creates a sense of urgency, whether claiming to be an IT help desk resetting a compromised login, or a bank fraud department stopping an unauthorised transfer, the victim has an urge to act. Scammers exploit this urgency, leaning on authority and fear to bypass critical thinking before the victim has time to double-check the facts. The…

items.title: What does the UAE’s next cyber challenge look like?

For years, security teams have focused on protecting people, devices, applications and infrastructure. That model still matters. But as AI becomes embedded more deeply into business processes, and as AI agents begin to take actions on behalf of users and organisations, the security challenge is becoming broader. The challenge now goes well beyond defending systems against attack. Organisations must govern increasingly autonomous systems: setting clear limits on what they can do, keeping their actions visible, and ensuring operations can continue when something goes wrong. items.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
items.summary: Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild. Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin. The flaws at issue are present in PHP , the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal , Magento , Joomla and WordPress . Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server. Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure. items.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
items.summary: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom. Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “ Rey ,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year. In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization. The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other…
